summary: Describes a simple out-of-band protocol for setting up the RPKI provisioning and publication protocols between two parties. A few XML messages exchange identities and keying material, and can be passed by any means with adequate integrity and authentication.

eli5.summary: Before two people start swapping letters, they exchange a small note introducing themselves and their stamps. This is that note.

questions: what is the rpki out-of-band setup protocol
what is a child_request in rpki
how does rpki publication referral work
subtitle: A small set of XML messages that lets two RPKI parties swap identities and keys before they start talking.

tldr.problem: Setting up the RPKI provisioning and publication protocols between two parties needs keying material and service URLs, and configuring them by hand was found to be error prone and confusing.
tldr.mechanism: Four XML messages (child request, parent response, publisher request, repository response) carry self-signed certificates, handles and service URLs, and a signed authorization token lets a parent refer a child to a repository.
tldr.outcome: The messages can travel by any means that gives acceptable integrity and authentication. The protocol only sets up relationships; it is not part of the provisioning or publication protocols themselves.

today: RFC 8183 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this setup protocol.

sections.title: Why a Setup Protocol Exists
sections.content:
RFC 8183 describes a small XML-based, out-of-band protocol that sets up relationships between parents and children in the RPKI provisioning protocol (RFC 6492) and between publishers and repositories in the RPKI publication protocol (RFC 8181).

Its basic job is public key exchange, in the form of self-signed X.509 certificates. Workshop experience showed it is simpler for users if the other configuration needed to bring up a new player is bundled into the same messages. The RFC says the protocol grew out of workshops that started in 2010, where manual configuration of keying material and service URLs was both error prone and unnecessarily confusing.

The transport is deliberately unspecified. The RFC lists a USB stick, a web interface secured with HTTPS, PGP-signed email, a T-shirt printed with a QR code, or a carrier pigeon. Because the point is key exchange, authentication and integrity of the exchange MUST be ensured by external means, typically tied to a business relationship.
sections.eli5: It is a handshake note for computers that need to start working together. How the note gets passed is up to you, as long as nobody can swap it for a fake.

sections.title: The Four Roles
sections.content:
The protocols being configured each have their own names for their actors, which gets confusing here, so this RFC uses its own terms:

  • Child: the client ("subject") in the provisioning protocol of RFC 6492.
  • Parent: the server ("issuer") in that protocol.
  • Publisher: the client in the publication protocol of RFC 8181.
  • Repository: the server in that protocol.

One entity can play several roles. In one of the simplest cases the child is also the publisher, and the parent is also the repository.
sections.eli5: Some people ask for things and some people give them. Sometimes one person does both jobs, so the note names each job separately.

sections.title: The Business PKI
sections.content:
Several RPKI provisioning protocols use signed Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) messages to authenticate their XML. Checking those messages needs X.509 certificates. The PKI holding them is separate from the RPKI and carries no RFC 3779 resources; the RFC calls it the Business PKI (BPKI), because its certificate relationships are likely to follow existing contracts.

In each exchange the sender includes a self-signed X.509 CA certificate. Its private key does not sign CMS messages directly. Instead it issues BPKI end-entity (EE) certificates, which go into the CMS messages and are used with the exchanged certificate to verify them.

The recommended way to use a received certificate is to cross-certify its public key and subject name under your own BPKI, with Basic Constraints cA = TRUE and pathLenConstraint = 0. That makes it a CA that may issue EE certificates but not other CA certificates. The RFC's example has Alice send her self-signed certificate to Bob, who cross-certifies it, so a later Alice EE certificate chains back to Bob's own trust anchor.

The RFC says the certificates exchanged at the time of writing were RSA keys of 2048 to 4096 bits, SHA-2 digests and a few common X.509v3 extensions, and that exact requirements are left to the two parties and may change over time.
sections.eli5: Each side shows the other a personal stamp. The receiver then makes an official copy under their own seal, so they can check later letters against it.

sections.title: The Four Messages
sections.content:
Every message is an XML element in the http://www.hactrn.net/uris/rpki/rpki-setup/ namespace with a version attribute; this document describes version 1. Certificates are the Base64 encoding of the DER form. A handle is a US-ASCII string of letters, digits and the characters slash, hyphen and underscore. An optional tag attribute is an opaque cookie that the responder echoes so the client can match replies to requests.

  • child_request: from child to parent. It carries a child_handle (only a hint the parent need not honor) and the child's self-signed certificate in child_bpki_ta.
  • parent_response: from parent to child. It gives the service_uri (an HTTP or HTTPS URL for up-down service), the parent's name for the child and for itself, and parent_bpki_ta. It may include an empty offer element (the parent offers publication service) and referral elements pointing to third-party repositories. If the parent and child handles differ, the parent wins.
  • publisher_request: from publisher to repository, with a handle hint and publisher_bpki_ta. It may carry a referral with an authorization token from the parent.
  • repository_response: from repository to publisher. It gives a service_uri for publication, the repository's name for the publisher, sia_base (the rsync:// URI at the base of the publication space allocated), an optional rrdp_notification_uri for the RRDP notification file (RFC 8182), and repository_bpki_ta.

When a request has a tag, the response MUST echo an identical tag; when it has none, the response MUST NOT include one.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of notes: "here is who I am" and "here is who I am and where to find me," once for borrowing resources and once for storing files.

sections.title: Authorization Tokens and Errors
sections.content:
The authorization element is a separate message, signed with CMS (eContentType id-ct-xml) and carried as Base64 text inside referral elements. Its authorized_sia_base attribute is the rsync:// URI of the namespace the referrer is delegating, and its text is the Base64 self-signed BPKI certificate of the entity receiving that delegation.

This is how a parent that runs no repository can send a child to someone else's. The repository checks the signature and that the certificate inside matches the requester's, but the repository operator still decides whether to grant service.

The optional error message answers any core message. Its reason is one of syntax-error (could not parse), authentication-failure (could not authenticate) or refused (declined the action), and it holds a verbatim copy of the offending message. Whether to use it depends on the implementation, for example whether a human or a program handles errors.
sections.eli5: A signed permission slip lets someone say "you may use a corner of my space over at that other building." The building owner still gets to say yes or no.

sections.title: The Alice, Bob and Carol Walk-Through
sections.content:
Alice is the root of an RPKI tree. Bob wants address and ASN resources from her, and Carol wants some of those from Bob. Alice offers publication service, and all three use it. Each generates a self-signed BPKI certificate.

Bob sends Alice a child_request. Alice already has 41 other children named Bob, so her parent_response renames him Bob-42 and includes an offer. Bob accepts by sending a publisher_request, and Alice answers with a repository_response that allocates space under her own publication space, so relying parties who rsync her products pick up Bob's automatically.

Carol sends Bob a child_request. Bob has no repository, so his parent_response has a referral (referrer Alice/Bob-42) holding a signed authorization for Carol's certificate. Carol sends that referral to Alice in a publisher_request, and Alice, after checking the signature and that the certificate matches Carol's, allocates a subtree to her.

The RFC notes that referrals could in theory chain indefinitely, but this had not been implemented or tested, and that perverse cases (Bob allowing Carol but not her own child) were deliberately ignored. A child need not accept any offer or referral, and where to publish is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Bob and Carol both want to keep their files at Alice's place. Alice says yes to Bob directly, and Bob writes Carol a signed note so Alice will let her in too.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The only security point the RFC makes is that the protocol's basic function is exchanging public keys to be used as BPKI trust anchors. Integrity and authentication of those exchanges MUST be ensured by external mechanisms that the protocol deliberately leaves unspecified. Anyone who can swap a certificate in transit can substitute their own identity.

The RFC requires no IANA actions. The RELAX NG schema in Appendix A is normative; if it disagrees with the prose, the schema wins.
sections.eli5: If someone can swap your note for a fake one on the way, they can pretend to be you. So the way you hand over the note has to be trustworthy.

messages.label: child_request
messages.note: Handle hint Bob plus his self-signed BPKI certificate.

messages.label: parent_response
messages.note: Handle Bob-42, service URI, her certificate and an offer of publication service.

messages.label: repository_response
messages.note: Publication service URI, sia_base and her certificate.

items.title: child_request
items.text: Child to parent: handle hint and child BPKI certificate.

items.title: parent_response
items.text: Parent to child: service URI, handles, parent certificate, offer or referral.

items.title: publisher_request
items.text: Publisher to repository: handle hint, certificate, optional referral.

items.title: repository_response
items.text: Repository to publisher: service URI, sia_base, optional RRDP URI, certificate.
